rows: Health professional’s conclusions and working assumptions that will guide treatment of the patient.

Shared plan informed by members of a coordinated care team that details conditions, needs, and goals along with strategies for addressing them.

Usage notes: Includes problems, health concerns, assessments, goals, and interventions from across care settings.

Examples include but are not limited to clinical care plans, condition-specific care plans, coordinated care plan.
Blood protein produced in response to and counteracting an antigen.
Proteins or sugars expressed on red blood cells used to determine an individuals' blood group.
Classification of blood based on the presence and absence of antibodies and inherited antigenic substances on the surface of red blood cells.
The name of the blood product originating from a human intended to be transplanted or infused into another (possibly the same) human (e.g., red blood cells, platelets, fresh frozen plasma).
BMI-for-age percentile shows how a child's weight compares to that of other children of the same age and sex.
The vertical measurement of an individual's stature from the feet to the top of the head when standing upright.
Temperature is a measure of the patient's ability to generate and get rid of heat.
The measurement of weight without heavy items located on the person.
Pulse oximetry is a test used to measure the oxygen level (oxygen saturation) of the blood.

Sequence of characters used to uniquely refer to a member of the care team. Examples include but are not limited to National Provider Identifier (NPI) and National Council of State Boards of Nursing Identifier (NCSBN ID).
Place where care is delivered by a care team member. Examples include but are not limited to clinic address, and location description.
Word or phrase that constitutes the distinctive designation of a care team member. Examples include but are not limited to given name, middle name, surname, and name suffix.
Responsibility of an individual within the care team. Examples include but are not limited to primary care physician and caregiver.
Phone or email contact information for a care team member.

Non-imaging or non-laboratory test.
Examples include but are not limited to electrocardiogram (ECG), visual acuity exam, macular exam, and graded exercise testing (GXT).
Place where a person is located or may be contacted.
Known or estimated year, month, and day of the patient's birth.
Known or estimated year, month, and day of the patient's death.
Unique identifier of an individual's email account that is used to send and receive email messages.
Patient's self-identification as Hispanic/ Latino or Non- Hispanic/ Non-Latino.
A personal name used before a family name.
Portion of one's personal name indicating familial or communal ties.
A second or subsequent given name, between the first given name and the family name or surname.
Name component following family name that may be used to describe a person's position in a family.
Numbers and symbols to contact an individual when using a phone.
Any first and last name an individual may have used in the past for any reason.
An individual’s response to the race question based upon self-identification.
Documentation of a specific instance of sex.
Date of first determination by a qualified professional of the presence of a problem or condition affecting a patient.
Date of subsiding or termination of a symptom, problem or condition.
Supporting evidence that is the basis for determining the condition.
Condition, diagnosis, or reason for seeking medical attention.

Social Determinants of Health-related health concerns, conditions, or diagnoses.
Examples include but are not limited to homelessness and food insecurity.

Tests that generate visual images and require interpretation by qualified professionals.

Examples include but are not limited to computed tomography-head, radiograph-chest, and ultrasound-pelvis.

Interpreted results of imaging tests.
Usage Note: Includes both structured and unstructured (narrative) components.
The genetic makeup of an individual's blood group, specifically the blood type and Rh factor.
The categorical or clinical assessment of the genetic variant data, where interpretation is necessary to fully understand the significance.

Assessment of a patient's physical, cognitive, or psychiatric disabilities.

Examples include but are not limited to American Community Survey, Veterans RAND Health Survey, and Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS).
Evaluation of a patient's emotional distress or physical discomfort utilizing a standardized instrument.

Assessment of a person’s ability to perform activities of daily living and activities across other situations and settings.

Examples include but are not limited to Functional Assessment Standardized Items (FASI) and Timed Up and Go (TUG).
Health-related issue or worry. Examples include but are not limited to weight gain and cancer risk.
Assessment or screening for the presence of a mental or behavioral problem. Examples include but are not limited to Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) and Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ).
Amount of a medication for each administration.
Units of measure of a medication. Examples include but are not limited to milligram (mg) and milliliter (mL).
Pharmacologic agent used in the diagnosis, cure, mitigation, treatment, or prevention of disease.
Pharmacologic category for an agent believed to cause a harmful or undesired physiologic response following exposure.
Pharmacologic agent believed to cause a harmful or undesired physiologic response following exposure.

Non-pharmacologic agent believed to cause a harmful or undesired physiologic response following exposure.
Examples include but are not limited to latex, eggs, pollen, and peanuts.
Harmful or undesired physiologic response following exposure to a substance
Coded diagnoses associated with an episode of care.
Place or setting where the patient went after a hospital stay or encounter.
Sequence of characters by which an encounter is known.
Place where a patient’s care is delivered.

Date/times related to an encounter.
Examples include but are not limited to scheduled appointment time, check in time, and start and stop times.
Category of health care service. Examples include but are not limited to office visit, telephone assessment, and home visit.
Physical location of available services or resources.
Sequence of characters representing a physical place of available services or resources.
Word or words by which a facility is known.

Category of service or resource available in a location.

Examples include but are not limited to hospital, laboratory, pharmacy, ambulatory clinic, long-term and post-acute care facility, and food pantry.
Vaccine product administered, planned, or reported.

Desired outcomes of patient’s care.

Examples include but are not limited to blood pressure control, functional ability, and nutrition.

Time and/or date an activity is performed.

Examples include but are not limited to vaccine or medication administration times, surgery start time, time ultrasound performed, and laboratory specimen collection time.
Date that the blood product originating from a human was or is intended to be transplanted or infused into another (possibly the same) human (e.g., red blood cells, platelets, fresh frozen plasma).
Activity performed for or on a patient as part of the provision of care.
Analysis of specimens derived from humans which provide information for the diagnosis, prevention, treatment of disease, or assessment of health.
Documented findings of a tested specimen including structured and unstructured components
